title: The poem, closed
hookLine: the life once more, now in verse

cards: Back in year one, the Buddha's life came to us in plain pieces: a birth, the sights on the road, a night ride, a tree, a first teaching, a last journey.

This block told the same life again, slowly, through one poet's eyes. Same story, different light. It's like walking a road you know by heart, but at dawn, with someone who stops to point at things you'd walked past.
Today, one last walk down the whole road, and a look at what the verse added.

teach.h: THE PALACE: WALLS MADE OF LOVE.
teach.b: First, the palace. A queen's dream, a birth in a grove, an old sage weeping because he won't live to hear the boy teach. A father who fills the palace with music because he is afraid.
In the poem, the walls are made of love, and that's what makes them hard to leave. Second, the road out. The sights the king tried to hide.
The worms in the plowed furrow, grieved for like family. A refused request, a sleeping palace, gates that open on their own, a horse and a faithful attendant sent home.

teach.h: THE ROAD OUT: EVERY GOODBYE HURTS.
teach.b: The poem lets every goodbye hurt.
Third, the search and the night. Arguments from ministers, half a kingdom offered by a king, teachers who are good but not final, a bowl of milk-rice after the fasting.
Then Mara with his flowered bow and his army, scattered, and a night of knowing, watch by watch, until dawn. Fourth, the turning and the end. Five old companions who rise despite themselves.
Friends, fire-keepers, kings, a great ascetic arriving late. And in the Tibetan and Chinese, the rest: the last journey, the sala trees, the relics shared.

teach.h: THE WHEEL, THE ARRIVALS, THE END.
teach.b: That's the life, retold. What did the verse add? Not new facts, mostly.
It added time to feel things. A father's fear.
A wife's question. A prince's grief over worms. In the poem of Nanda, the poet said he wrote so people would stay for the teaching.
All these days on one poem is a long stay. Next, the path turns from the teacher to the people who followed him, beginning with two friends at a festival.

how: The Buddha's life is retold again and again in Buddhist cultures: in temple murals and carvings, in festival plays and chanting, and in children's books, each telling choosing its own scenes and its own light.

games.q: you have five lines to tell the Buddha's whole life to a friend. which line do you start with?
games.why: the poem opens with his parents, the queen's dream and the birth in a grove, and walks the whole road from there to the relics.

practice: Tell the Buddha's life to yourself in five plain lines, one breath each: born a prince; saw age, sickness and death; left home; woke up under a tree; taught until the end.
Use your own words if they come, then let the lines go and sit with whatever stays.

wordCard.voice: The poem. Ashvaghosha's life of the Buddha, from the palace to the relics, told in verse so listeners would stay. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit kavya, the ornate court poetry the Buddhacarita is written in.

carryVoice: Your line: the life, retold. The same story, told slowly enough to feel. That's day seven hundred twenty-four.
